en: The *Sūtra on the Dhāraṇī of the Gateways to Boundless Births*,
translated by the Elder General-Master Zhisheng of Zhixiang Monastery on Mount Zhongnan.
Thus have I heard.
At one time the Buddha was staying at the Great Forest Monastery in the city of Vaiśālī,
together with a great assembly of bhikṣus numbering four billion two hundred million people.
There were eight billion bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
At that time, the World-Honored One reflected upon his own life-span,
knowing that in three months he would enter parinirvāṇa.
He then addressed the Elder Mahāmaudgalyāyana:
"You must proclaim throughout this trichiliocosm to all śramaṇas who seek the three vehicles."
They all came together at this Great Forest Monastery.
Thereupon, Maudgalyāyana respectfully received the Buddha’s instruction and,
by means of his supernormal powers, in a single thought-moment—
Reaching the summit of Mount Sumeru, he uttered a great sound,
causing all sentient beings throughout this trichiliocosm to hear and know it entirely.
And he spoke in verse:
"O sons of the Buddha, all throughout every world, listen well!
The Buddha now rains down the rain of Dharma; whoever desires it, let them all go there."
At that time, after Maudgalyāyana had spoken these verses,
four billion two hundred million koṭis of bhikṣus came to the vihāra.
Then, the Elder Śāriputra thought to himself:
"I shall now likewise, by means of my supernormal powers,
cause all the śramaṇas from every village to assemble here.
Having formed this thought, he immediately manifested his supernormal powers.
At that time, thirty billion hundred thousand śramaṇas gathered at the vihāra;
they prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to sit to one side.
Then the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, the Dharma Prince.
The Bodhisattva Free from All Sorrow,
the Bodhisattva Free from All Objects of Perception,
and the Bodhisattva Peak Eloquence of Inexhaustibility.
The Bodhisattva Abandoner of All Obscurations, the Bodhisattva Amoghadarśin,
and the Bodhisattva Savior from Evil Destinies.
Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva,
Gandhahastin Bodhisattva,
and Maitreya Bodhisattva.
"Good son, go to the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River.
Among them are all those bodhisattvas who are in their final birth before enlightenment (ekajātipratibaddha) and those bodhisattvas who are non-retrogressive (avaivartika)."
The Bodhisattvas who had attained the patience of non-arising were universally summoned to assemble at the Great Forest Monastery (Mahāvana-vihāra).
At that time, the Bodhisattvas received the holy command of the Buddha.
In each of those worlds where they went,
there were eight billion hundred thousand bodhisattvas in their final birth before enlightenment (*ekajātipratibaddha*),
and billions of hundred thousand bodhisattvas who were non-retrogressive (*avaivartika*).
Three billion bodhisattvas who had attained the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas,
and six billion bodhisattvas with pure resolve and liberation—
bodhisattva-mahāsattvas such as these all gathered for this assembly.
Furthermore, there were incalculable numbers of bodhisattvas who had first resolved their minds toward enlightenment,
as well as those bodhisattvas who were worthy vessels for the Dharma; all of them,
together with their peers, relied upon the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha.
Each came from their own native land, traveling through the air;
they paid homage to the Buddha and withdrew to stand to one side.
At that time, Śāriputra saw the various bodhisattvas.
Although the varieties and distinctions of their worlds differ,
they have all gathered together, traveling through the air in equal measure.
They conceived a doubt in their minds, wondering whether this was brought about by the power of the Tathāgata’s merit and spiritual authority.
For what reason have you come here?
We shall now question the Buddha,
so as to cause the assembly of bodhisattvas here to understand.
Upon hearing what the Buddha had taught, all their doubts and perplexities were entirely removed.
They attained unimpeded eloquence as vast as the sands of the Ganges,
and regarding the Dharma heard from all Tathāgatas, they received and upheld it without doubt or forgetfulness.
This continues until they attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Furthermore, it causes them to swiftly obtain the four kinds of pure and inexhaustible Dharma-gates of a bodhisattva. What are these four?
That is to say: the purity of sentient beings,
the purity of the Dharma-gate,
and the purity of eloquent exposition.
They praise the purity of the Buddha-field and further attain four kinds of excellent qualities. What are these four? They are:
excellence of physical marks, excellence of oral marks, [excellence of mental marks, and excellence of conduct].
The mental characteristics are excellent, and the skillful means are excellent.
Furthermore, one attains entry into the four dharanī-doors. What are these four?
These are the so-called dhāraṇī gateways of upholding the inexhaustible;
the dhāraṇī gateway of penetrating the profound Dharma;
and the dhāraṇī gateway of skillfully entering the faculties of sentient beings.
The Dharani Door that Universally Discerns the Retribution of Good and Evil Karmic Actions.
At that time, because of this doubt, Śāriputra,
according to what he had conceived and what he had pondered, [addressed the Buddha].
He addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, what is the movement of thought and the application of observation in a bodhisattva?
What is the pure wisdom and immeasurable discernment of a bodhisattva?"
"I only pray that the Tathāgata will expound it for me.
The Buddha said, "Excellent, excellent, Śāriputra!
You now desire to benefit and bring peace and happiness to immeasurable sentient beings."
Out of compassion for humans and devas, so that they may experience happiness,
you now inquire about this meaning from the Tathāgata.
Śāriputra, do you wish to cause beginner bodhisattvas to awaken to and understand the profound Dharma?
To swiftly attain immeasurable eloquence and skillful means,
and to quickly achieve *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*,
you should listen attentively and reflect upon it well.
"I shall now analyze and explain this for you.
Śāriputra replied, "So be it, World-Honored One; we shall receive your instruction and listen.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra:
If bodhisattvas seek unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment,
they should give rise to a vast mind that is free from attachment,
without grasping, and without abandoning.
Receive, uphold, recite, and contemplate this dhāraṇī.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke the dhāraṇī, saying:
*tadātve dhaṃ* (1) *aṇamaṇa* (2) *akṣimakṣi* (3) *saman*.

Lri (repha-virāma) svāhā. The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"If a bodhisattva practices this dhāraṇī, they should not discriminate between the conditioned and the unconditioned."
Furthermore, one neither grasps nor clings to them, neither increases nor decreases them;
they are not established nor destroyed, neither joined nor dispersed, neither arising nor ceasing.
Nor does one dwell upon past, future, or present phenomena.
Nor do they accumulate or grasp at any phenomena;
rather, they should contemplate the Buddhas as being neither form nor formless.
It is neither with marks nor without marks.
A bodhisattva should not, like the followers of the two vehicles, grasp at the form-body (rūpakāya) of a Buddha.
Why is this? Because śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas...
One perceives the marks of the Buddha’s physical body adorned with majesty, its radiance shining brilliantly;
yet this is composed of the four great elements— blood, flesh, sinews, and bones— nourished by the parents through birth, food, and drink,
and is thus impermanent and subject to decay.
The Buddha’s form-body (rūpakāya) consists of suffering, affliction, and impurity;
it is not so for the bodhisattva. Why is this?
Because the body of the Tathāgata is devoid of the characteristic of arising.
For the sake of all sentient beings, regarding all phenomena,
he gathers the provisions of wisdom through the illumination of non-clarity,
manifesting the dharmakāya as having the characteristics of space and the characteristic of non-arising.
The Dharma-body of the Tathāgata takes the characteristic of non-arising as its aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha).
Furthermore, because it is the essence of all phenomena by virtue of the profound meaning of the characteristic of non-arising.
However, bodhisattvas should not apprehend the marks of the Tathāgata by means of non-form;
if they were to apprehend the marks of the Tathāgata by means of non-form, they would be the same as the śrāvakas,
who claim that the Buddha has entered into the extinction of parinirvāṇa.
The physical body is severed and extinguished, never to be born again;
it is not so with the Bodhisattva. Why is this?
Because the body of the Tathāgata possesses the characteristic of inexhaustibility.
For the sake of all sentient beings, they manifest a form-body through the illumination of non-illumination regarding all phenomena;
they gather the provisions of merit by taking dharmas as signs.
Because the Tathāgata’s form-body possesses inexhaustible characteristics,
this constitutes the inexhaustible aggregate of form.
Therefore, all phenomena likewise possess inexhaustible characteristics.
If the realms of sentient beings have not yet been fully delivered, the Tathāgata constantly manifests inexhaustible form-bodies;
he may manifest as the body of a Buddha, or the body of a bodhisattva, or the body of a pratyekabuddha, or the body of a śrāvaka.
He manifests as the body of Brahmā, the body of Śakra, the body of Maheśvara, and the body of Nārāyaṇa;
or again, he appears in the form of kings, ministers, elders, merchant leaders, and skilled physicians.
They may manifest in the forms of śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās;
or they may manifest as men, women, boys, or girls.
Even to manifest in the bodies of birds and beasts,
all is for the purpose of delivering and liberating all sentient beings;
it is through skillful means that these are displayed.
Furthermore, a bodhisattva should not, like the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas,
grasp at the thirty-two marks of a Tathāgata by thinking that the Buddha’s physical body is born of parents and is a composite of flesh and bone.
It is not so for the Bodhisattva. Why?
Because the body of the Tathāgata has the characteristic of space;
since it lacks the characteristic of arising, it is also not luminously radiant.
For the sake of all sentient beings, he gathers the provisions of wisdom.
Within all phenomena, he manifests the Dharma-body;
this Buddha-Dharma-body is characterized by non-entry.
Because they possess the characteristic of inexhaustibility, he manifests the thirty-two marks;
because the profound meaning of the characteristic of non-arising is the essence of all dharmas.
However, bodhisattvas should not be like śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas,
who grasp at the Buddha as having non-characteristics,
namely, that the Buddha has entered into the quiescent nirvāṇa.
All marks are extinguished and do not arise again;
it is not so with the Bodhisattva. Why is this?
Because the body of the Tathāgata possesses inexhaustible marks.
For the sake of all sentient beings, he manifests a form-body through the illumination of non-illumination regarding all phenomena;
by taking dharmas as signs, he accumulates the provisions of merit.
Because the physical body of the Tathāgata possesses inexhaustible characteristics,
and because the thirty-two marks possess inexhaustible characteristics,
all dharmas likewise possess inexhaustible characteristics.
If the realm of sentient beings has not yet been fully delivered and liberated,
the Tathāgata constantly manifests with a body adorned by various marks and radiant light;
within those marks, [he remains].
Furthermore, he manifested various extraordinary and immeasurable marks.
What were these marks?
They were the Buddhas of the ten directions and their respective lands.
Within those marks, everything is reflected; if there are sentient beings who see or hear this, they will gain faith, understanding, and awakening, and their bodhicitta will grow.
For this reason, a bodhisattva should not apprehend the Tathāgata by means of non-marks.
Furthermore, a bodhisattva should not, like the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas,
grasp at the eighty minor marks of the Tathāgata,
up to and including the mark of cessation as described above.
If the realm of sentient beings has not yet been fully delivered and liberated,
the Tathāgata constantly adorns his body with the secondary marks (anuvyañjana) and illuminates it with radiance;
within those marks, [he manifests further].
Furthermore, he manifests various extraordinary and inexhaustible marks.
What are these marks? They are as follows:
"When I first resolved to attain enlightenment..."
I was a king named Prabhāsa,
and it was during that time that I encountered the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara, who bestowed upon me the prediction of my future enlightenment,
continuing thus through the third asaṃkhyeya kalpa.
All the ascetic practices performed during that interval appear within each of the secondary marks (anuvyañjana).
If there are sentient beings who see or hear this, [they shall attain liberation].
Through faith, understanding, and awakening, one should cultivate the bodhicitta.
For this reason, a bodhisattva should not grasp at the signs of the disappearance of the secondary marks (anuvyañjana),
nor should they dwell upon their family or retinue.
As for morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation:
they are not practiced and not attained, nor is anything obtained therein;
they are neither defiled nor pure, neither wise nor foolish.
Furthermore, there is no teaching of the purity of selflessness or the purity of the absence of sentient beings;
there is neither benefiting oneself nor benefiting others, neither the arising of dharmas nor the cessation of dharmas,
and likewise no purification of the actions of body, speech, and mind.
Nor does it belong to the past, future, or present;
it is not for oneself, nor for another.
Śāriputra, this is the bodhisattva.
Beginning with the observation of the Tathāgata’s form-body (rūpakāya) as well as the aggregates (skandha),
elements (dhātu), and sense-bases (āyatana), when one achieves such realization, one enters this Dharma-gate, being remembered by all Buddhas.
At that time, the Bodhisattva, by means of this dharma-gate,
purifies the nature of bodhi and is able to know the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed, truly pure bodhi-dharmakāya,
which is the very essence of the dharmakāya of all Tathāgatas.
This is not the sphere of activity for ordinary fools, nor can it be known by those of the two vehicles or by novice bodhisattvas. Why is this?

Because such individuals take pleasure in and are attached to the physical body, its marks and signs, as well as the aggregates, sense bases, and elements, even up to the primary and secondary marks of a buddha.
Because they practice in this way,
one should know that the beginner bodhisattvas of the past purified the nature of enlightenment through this dharma-gate.
It is all for the sake of compassionately regarding all sentient beings that one cultivates the physical body, the aggregates, the elements, and the sense bases;
one should know that the dharma-gate of bodhi is established in this way.
Why is this? Because this physical body accords with worldly conventions;
through it, sentient beings make offerings to the Triple Gem and cultivate the bodhisattva practices of the six pāramitās and the four means of attraction (saṃgrahavastu).
Thereupon, by means of this Dharma-gate,
the bodhisattva transforms it into all internal and external phenomena of the world—
whether as the aggregates, elements, and sense bases, or as the thirty-two marks and eighty secondary characteristics.
Even unto parents and kinsmen;
the aggregates of ethical discipline, concentration, and wisdom; the aggregate of liberation and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation;
and all medicinal herbs, flowers, fruits, nectar, and the sprouts and crops of the hundred grains.
For the sake of benefiting sentient beings, he establishes them through skillful means.
If a bodhisattva, from the very first phrase,
awakens to and understands the pure dharma-body of bodhi.
Furthermore, one should know that the establishment of the form-body (rūpakāya) according to the subsequent phrase is precisely what is authorized by the Omniscient One. Why is this?
Because ordinary, ignorant sentient beings accumulate worldly karma.
Because they are attached to "what belongs to me" and do not understand the ultimate truth, they are not called the mind of omniscience.
Although the two vehicles possess knowledge of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*),
because it is not the correct view that extinguishes the seeds of birth and death, [they are not so called].
Nor does one praise the mind of omniscience.
The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, fully know both the ultimate and conventional truths;
with inexhaustible wisdom and perfected vows and aspirations, they have attained great enlightenment.
He further enters the samādhi of all roots of goodness;
therefore, he accords with the mind of omniscience. Why is this?
Because ordinary, ignorant beings, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas [do not].
Furthermore, the supreme merit obtained by all bodhisattvas is entirely brought about by the virtues of the Buddhas.
If the Tathāgata were not to attain equal and perfect enlightenment, [these would not exist].
There is nothing that does not arise from the power of the *dhāraṇī* of the gateways to the infinite.
You should know that this sutra is the root from which all roots of goodness are born,
and it is the treasury in which all dharma-gates are accumulated.
The lineage is stainless and transcends the armies of Māra.
Śāriputra, if any bodhisattvas hear this *Sūtra of the Dharani of the Gateways to Boundless Birth*, [they shall attain this].
They shall all become non-retrogressive from unsurpassed bodhi.
Why is this? Because this sutra fully reveals the conduct of all Buddhas and praises their merits;
it is capable of destroying [the afflictions] of all sentient beings.
The Dharma-method of the karmic activities of birth and death, free from defilement.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Do not take pleasure in or become attached to any phenomena; all dharmas are empty."
Do not give rise to discrimination regarding the enlightenment of all Buddhas;
Regarding enlightenment and nirvana, let no doubt arise in the mind.
If one can practice this way, one will swiftly attain dhāraṇī.
Hearing this sūtra, one practices wisdom that is empty, signless, unarisen, and unceasing;
such a bodhisattva who upholds this scripture shall swiftly realize awakening, having deeply understood immeasurable dharmas.
One shall be born in the lands of all Buddhas and draw near to the Most Victorious Honored Ones;
if one attains this dhāraṇī, one will certainly comprehend the profound meaning and purpose,
never giving rise to fear or retreat, and shall uphold the inexhaustible Dharma.
The teachings spoken by all Buddhas of the ten directions, one hears them all completely;
having heard them, one receives and maintains them all, wearing them upon the crown of the head and practicing them accordingly.
If one receives and maintains this sutra, regarding its words, phrases, and names—
And regarding the sublime meanings therein explained, they never have any doubt or forgetfulness;
like the light of the sun and moon, there is nothing they do not illuminate.
Having fully understood this Dharma-gate, they penetrate immeasurable meanings.
By reciting and upholding this sutra, one will spontaneously be able to understand all the most supreme dharmas. Even if,
throughout an entire kalpa, all sentient beings were to [expound] the wondrous gateway of the dhāraṇī...
Whatever deep doubts there may be, Ask them all of those who uphold this sutra.
At that time, the Bodhisattvas who uphold the sutra Shall all explain and expound for them;
The net of doubt shall be entirely removed, For the wisdom of these Bodhisattvas is inexhaustible.
Because they love and delight in this sutra, they are able to swiftly approach Bodhi.
Such true children of the Buddha protect and uphold the secret treasury;
by maintaining this dharani, all sentient beings will revere and remember them.
All Buddhas together extol them, Their fame resounds throughout the ten directions;
Because they uphold this sutra, When their life is about to end,
They shall see eight billion buddhas Extend their hands to receive and escort them.
They all spoke these words: "You should go to my land;
by reciting and upholding this sutra, you shall receive such blessings as these.
Even for the sins one might commit over hundreds of thousands of billions of kalpas, they shall be extinguished."
By reciting this dhāraṇī for one month, one becomes entirely pure;
though a bodhisattva may diligently cultivate all merits for a hundred million kalpas,
the merit of reciting this sūtra for one month surpasses that.
Because the sutras of samādhi and dhāraṇī— consisting of wholesome mindfulness,
wisdom, and diligence— are constantly present before them,
even all sentient beings throughout the three realms, up to the stage of a Tathāgata, would at once become entirely Māras.
By reciting and upholding this sutra, none shall be able to create obstacles;
herein the explanations of all dharma-gates are set forth, and through them,
omniscience is proclaimed, whereby one attains perfect enlightenment.
Because I heard this sutra, Dīpaṃkara bestowed upon me a prophecy, declaring:
"You shall become a Buddha and liberate all sentient beings.
At that time, I beheld Buddhas whose number was like the sands of the Ganges.
Hearing the Dharma preached by all Buddhas, one is able to understand it all completely;
if one wishes to receive and uphold the teachings spoken by all Buddhas,
one should diligently practice and study this sutra to swiftly achieve such power.
The sublime adornment of the buddha-field, the great assembly of all the noble ones,
their radiant marks and wondrous lineages—
all are obtained from this sutra. If a person, for seven days, contemplates this sutra with focused attention, [they shall attain these].
Eighty billion buddhas have preached such a Dharma as this:
"Do not think with perverse thoughts; be careful not to think. One should not think, nor should one think;
one should think correctly with wisdom, and thus quickly attain this sutra."
Diligently cultivate this dharma-gate; do not fear that bodhi is far away.
Just as one reaches an island of rare treasures and gathers all manner of jewels at will, if you uphold this dhāraṇī, do not say there is no karmic reward for goodness.
Possessing the joys of humans and devas, it is not difficult to approach the rank of a Buddha;
if you wish to swiftly attain Buddhahood, you should uphold this sutra,
and you will ultimately and certainly obtain the unsurpassed, great Bodhi.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"If a bodhisattva accomplishes four dharmas, they will certainly attain this dhāraṇī. What are these four?
First, not delighting in sensual desires."
Second, not giving rise to envy;
third, being able to relinquish everything toward all sentient beings without any malice or affliction;
fourth, being joyful day and night and deeply delighting in seeking the Dharma.
Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva accomplishes these four dharmas, they obtain this dhāraṇī.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
“Sensual desire, burning with intense fervor, Can become the cause for the hells.”
The Māra-king creates these obstacles to the Path; one should swiftly distance oneself from them.
Through indolence, one commits various transgressions, and by means of evil karma, one falls into the hells, wandering within them for many eons without rest.
One should not give rise to envy; one should sever gain and fame, and look upon the poor with eyes of compassion. Therefore, one attains such a station as this.
All who engage in disputes, those with greedy hearts and stingy minds—[may they find peace].
If one can completely sever [all afflictions], one shall attain such a Dharma as this.
By diligently seeking the Dharma day and night, remaining free from anger toward sentient beings,
and single-mindedly delighting in this sutra, one will swiftly be able to obtain this sutra.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, if a bodhisattva accomplishes four dharmas, they will obtain this dhāraṇī. What are these four?
First, dwelling in the practice of a silent aranya.
Second, awakening to and entering into the profound patience regarding the Dharma (*gambhīradharmanidhyānakṣānti*).
Third, not delighting in fame or gain.
Fourth, being able to relinquish all cherished things, even up to one's own body and life.
When a bodhisattva accomplishes these four dharmas, they obtain this dhāraṇī.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Constantly practicing in araṇyas, as praised by all Buddhas."
Diligently practice the patience of the profound Dharma, as if your head were on fire;
awaken to and enter into the meaning of the profound Dharma.
Do not disparage others, and do not be attached to home, fame, profit, or gain.
Do not give rise to craving for various riches and treasures;
delight in few desires and contentment, like a bird that has no store of provisions.
Having already obtained this human body, one should constantly cultivate virtuous conduct.
Having left the home life, one abandons the root of suffering; how excellent it is to attain the Buddha-dharma!
All afflictions such as pride and the like are rendered completely pure.
One should diligently practice reverence and honor the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.
Those who lose mindfulness and wisdom through greed for gain,
and likewise lose their faith and practice— such persons as these are very far from Bodhi;
therefore, one should abandon fame and profit.
Practicing the pure precepts, With right view and compassionate conduct.
Furthermore, Śāriputra,
if a bodhisattva accomplishes four dharmas, they will obtain this dhāraṇī.
What are these four?
They are the entry into the meaning of eight syllables.
What are the eight syllables?
The first is the syllable *pa*.
It is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*),
the meaning of entering into the selflessness of all phenomena.
The second is the syllable *la*.
It enters the Tathāgata’s unborn *dharmakāya*,
for it is the non-manifestation of the accumulation of wisdom-merit, being without any characteristic of entry.
Taking the characteristic of non-arising as the form-body (rūpakāya),
and taking the characteristic of inexhaustibility as the meaning of the aggregates of form (rūpaskandha) and the sense-bases (āyatana).
Third is the syllable MA.
The syllable "Ka" signifies the meaning of entering into the sense that the phenomena of wisdom and ignorance are of the same nature.

Fourth is the syllable "Gha," which signifies the meaning of entering into the sense that although one discriminates between karmic retribution and the absence of karmic retribution, there is in fact no such distinction.
Fifth is the syllable Ja,
which awakens one to the meaning of entering into the non-arising and non-ceasing of birth, old age, sickness, and death.
Sixth is the syllable Dha.
One awakens to the dharma-body of the dhāraṇī as empty, signless, wishless, and quiescent like nirvāṇa, thereby opening understanding and entering its meaning.
Seventh is the syllable *śa* (pronounced with a retroflex *ṣa*):
it is the characteristic of dwelling in the tranquility of *śamatha*.
Through vipaśyanā, one correctly perceives the characteristics of all phenomena.
How then can one abide in tranquil concentration?
One should apply oneself with diligence, without interruption, day and night.
When contemplating the form of the Buddha, one should not grasp at signs;
rather, one should practice *vipaśyanā* and see correctly with wisdom.
If a practitioner sees the Buddha appearing and takes him to be the actual Buddha, [this is an error].
One should reflect thus: "From which direction does this Buddha whom I see come?
Does he come from the east, west, south, north, the four intermediate directions, or from above or below?
If this Buddha were created by a person..."
One should reflect thus:
"Is this Buddha made of clay or wood?
Or is it fashioned from gold or copper?"
Having observed in this way, one knows that the Buddha seen is merely due to my having contemplated the image of the Buddha within the vihāra and recollecting it day and night.
Therefore, this Buddha is always manifest before one's eyes.
From this, one should know that when I constantly see and hear all phenomena and take them to be real,
they all arise from the recollections of my own mind.
This is the Bodhisattva’s first cultivation of the non-abiding concentration (*apratiṣṭhita-samādhi*).
If, during the initial stage, the Bodhisattva has attained a slight degree of clarity through the contemplative mind they have cultivated, [they proceed as follows].
One should immediately collect the mind and apply effort until one can know that all phenomena existing in the entire world arise entirely without departing from one's own mind.
This is the second virtuous characteristic of a bodhisattva: non-abiding in meditative concentration.
Furthermore, the bodhisattva should observe in this way:
"To whom does this essence of mindfulness belong?"
One should know that it is merely the dependent-arising mind which serves as the basis for the imagined nature;
one should further understand that this mind does not possess even so much as a hair’s tip of intrinsic existence.
This is the Bodhisattva’s third patience regarding the inability to remain in meditative concentration.
Immediately following this, he then gives rise to the concentration of mastery.
Having arisen from this concentration, [he...]

This is the Bodhisattva’s fourth stage: the non-abiding concentration on the unsurpassed dharmas of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). Among the dharmas of conventional truth, the bodhicitta is supreme.
This is the mind of the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature).
One enters universally into the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
This perfected nature is the naturally pure suchness (*prakṛti-viśuddha-tathatā*),
and this suchness is the mind of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya-citta*).
Why is this? Because the ultimate truth (paramārthasatya) possesses two characteristics.
What are these two characteristics?
They are the characteristic of non-arising (anutpāda-lakṣaṇa).
Because the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body is the essence of pure continuity,
and because it is characterized by inexhaustibility,
he manifests the Tathāgata’s form-body as the essence of the continuity of the marks and signs of physical excellence.
Having clarified the pure essence of the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body,
and having further clarified the essence of the manifestation of the marks and signs of the form-body (rūpakāya),
the Bodhisattva then understands the liberation-dharma-gate of the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu).
Seeing what has never been seen before, his heart gives rise to joy;
this is the Bodhisattva’s attainment of the stage of supreme joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*).
Why is suchness (*tathatā*) the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*)?
This perfected nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva) also extends to the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya).
Within the ultimate sense, greed, hatred,
and delusion are primordially empty and quiescent, with nothing to be abandoned.
The pure dharmakāya, within the ultimate sense,
is primordially ever-present and cannot be augmented;
this is realized through the mind of non-apprehension by means of right view.
By accumulating the provisions for wisdom and pacifying all unwholesome dharmas,
the Dharma-body of the Buddhas is manifested.
Because one performs all wholesome dharmas by means of right view,
the form bodies (rūpakāya) of the Buddhas manifest. How, then,
is the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva) also the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya)?
Because nature itself arises from the habituation of causes that are inherently non-existent,
it is free from the clinging to existence;
yet, because phenomena persist, it is not non-existence.
It is devoid of grasping at non-existence.
Furthermore, what is the nature of the thoroughly imagined?
It is the five aggregates, the twelve bases, and the eighteen elements.
Furthermore, one should know that abiding in the gateway of ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya),
the various categories of aggregates (skandha) and so forth that are perceived are merely the result of the habitual tendencies (vāsanā) of ordinary, ignorant beings.
Recollection and mental objects do not truly exist; therefore,
the Bodhisattva understands that within the aggregates, elements, and sense bases,
the Dharma-body manifests throughout all phenomena.
Once the bodhisattva has understood that those aggregates, elements,
and sense bases are merely what is seen by the deluded minds of ordinary beings,
he nevertheless employs these very things to gather all sentient beings and cultivate the bodhisattva practice.
Therefore, when a bodhisattva perceives the aggregates, elements, and sense bases,
they see the physical body with its marks and signs as the manifestation of all essential natures, characteristics, and provisions. How, then,
does one contemplate the image of the Buddha while also abiding in the gateway of ultimate truth?
One should form this thought: "The image of the Buddha that I now see does not possess the marks of the Buddha's actual nature;
it is merely due to the present conditions of my observation of the image."
Upon seeing the image of the Buddha, one attains meditative absorption (samādhi).
By analogy, one knows that all phenomena (dharmas) are likewise so.
For this reason, one beholds the image of the Buddha.
It should not be understood as being entirely non-existent.
One should know that the syllable *śa* and all phenomena are without distinction in their non-existence; they are identical in their entry into the meaning of the Dharma-gate.
Eighth is the syllable *kṣa*.
All phenomena are empty, neither arising nor ceasing. Why?
Because one awakens to and understands that all phenomena are originally empty and quiescent, and that their intrinsic nature is *nirvāṇa*; this is the meaning of entry.
One should uphold the meaning of these eight phrases in this manner.
In whichever direction this scripture may be found,
one should honor, revere, and make offerings to it.
Every half-month, they shall recite and expound it;
and if they see anyone studying this sutra,
they shall praise and encourage them.
"Śāriputra, if there are bodhisattvas who cultivate these four dharmas,
they will attain this dhāraṇī.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
Constantly recollecting these eight words, One should copy and uphold this sutra,
And preach it every half-month; Diligently transforming all sentient beings,
Thereby drawing near to the rank of a Buddha, Whose wisdom becomes exceedingly vast.
In the lands of the ten directions, one shall personally behold all the Tathāgatas;
then, in the presence of those Buddhas, one shall study the dharmas practiced by the Buddhas,
firmly uphold their teachings, and utterly eliminate all evils.
Furthermore, Śāriputra,
if there are bodhisattvas who practice and study such dhāraṇīs,
they shall obtain four kinds of benefits from the roots of goodness.
What are the four?
First, the Buddhas of the ten directions will protect and sustain this person.
Second, they will ultimately be free from the disturbances and afflictions of Māras.
Third, all karmic obstacles of evil deeds will be swiftly purified.
Fourth, one will quickly attain subtle and uninterrupted eloquence.
Śāriputra, if there is a bodhisattva...
By upholding such a dhāraṇī, one obtains these benefits of the Dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Because of upholding this sutra, The Buddhas of the ten directions will protect and mindfully remember you."
All the hosts of Māras shall be unable to cause affliction;
heavy suffering and various karmic obstructions shall be swiftly exhausted without remainder.
One should quickly be able to attain understanding through this dhāraṇī.
Hearing this sutra praised, reading and reciting it, copying it,
and practicing according to its teachings, one will swiftly realize the fruit of Bodhi.
Thus spoke the Buddha to Śāriputra.
In the distant past, immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago,
there was a Buddha named Ratnottama-Tejorāja-kalparāja Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.
He appeared in the world.
Śāriputra, at the time when the Tathāgata King of the Jewel-Victorious-Resplendent-Past-Aeon was approaching parinirvāṇa,
there was a wheel-turning sage king named Nakṣatradhara.
The king, endowed with the seven treasures, ruled over the four continents.
This king had a son named Acintyaguṇaviśeṣa.
At that time, the prince was sixteen years of age.
At the time of the Buddha King of the Jewel-Supreme Kalpa,
he first heard this dhāraṇī and practiced it with diligent application;
subsequently, for a period of seventy thousand years, he continued his cultivation.
He renounced his body, life, wealth, and royal throne; furthermore,
for seventy thousand years, he dwelt alone in secluded tranquility,
sitting in the full lotus posture with his side never touching the ground.
In the presence of ninety-nine billion hundred-thousand nayutas of Tathāgatas,
he heard this sutra being preached and received and upheld it in its entirety.
At that time, the prince immediately left the household life and became a renunciant.
For nine thousand years, by means of this *Anantamukha-dhāraṇī*,
he extensively expounded its meaning for the sake of sentient beings;
and thereafter, the prince-monk was born in a subsequent life.
He converted eighty billion nayutas of hundreds of thousands of sentient beings,
causing them all to dwell securely in the path of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*;
some even attained the stage of non-retrogression.
At that time, there was a householder in that assembly named Candradhvaja.
Having heard this exposition of the *Anantamukha-dhāraṇī*,
by the power of the roots of goodness and merit arising from his sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*), he...
Having encountered and reverently made offerings to nine hundred million Buddhas, World-Honored Ones,
one obtains this supreme dharma of dhāraṇī,
which is the most excellent among all discourses.
Furthermore, he attained the foremost uninterrupted eloquence;
having made offerings to all Buddhas throughout three kalpas,
at the conclusion of those three kalpas, he realized unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
He was named Dīpaṃkara.
Śāriputra, that prince of inconceivable merit and supreme virtue, the bhikṣu of that time,
is now the Buddha Amitāyus.
Śāriputra, when I and the bodhisattvas of this Bhadrakalpa were practicing the bodhisattva path,
we all heard this dhāraṇī and rejoiced in it with our whole hearts.
By virtue of this root of goodness resulting from sympathetic joy,
one transcends the cycle of birth and death for forty hundred thousand kalpas within the world;
furthermore, one makes offerings to and reveres nine hundred million Tathāgatas.
Thereafter, one shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Śāriputra, if you wish to quickly attain great Bodhi, you should receive and uphold this dhāraṇī.
If, moreover, one is unable to receive and uphold it,
one should simply give rise to sympathetic joy. Why is this so?
By means of these roots of goodness, one will certainly attain the stage of non-retrogression,
up until the attainment of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*;
how much more so for those who receive, uphold, recite, read, and transcribe it!
If one extensively analyzes and expounds this for others,
the merit obtained will be inconceivable and immeasurable;
no sentient being is able to fathom it.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"If there are those who hear this sutra, Transcribe it, give rise to sympathetic joy,
Recite and uphold it, And extensively explain it to others..."
The merit they have attained cannot be measured by sentient beings;
throughout immeasurable kalpas, they will receive inexhaustible blessings.
Wherever these bodhisattvas are born, they shall always behold the Buddhas.
Having attained inconceivable faith and skillfully understood the meaning of the profound sutras,
one who previously had doubts or obstructions regarding the scriptures will be able to awaken on their own;
from this, they shall swiftly achieve the fruit of unsurpassed bodhi.
The dhāraṇīs, supernormal powers, and meditative concentrations— All these are inexhaustible;
they have fully realized the profound patience of the Dharma (dharmakṣānti) And are always in the presence of all Tathāgatas.
I recall that in past lives, I heard this sūtra being preached.
Having paid homage to Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, he attained the Unsurpassed Way;
that Elder Candhadhvaja became the Buddha named Dīpaṃkara-guṇaviśeṣa,
and the Bhikṣu became Amitāyus Buddha.
I, together with immeasurable bodhisattvas of this Bhadrakalpa,
have all heard this sutra; with deep resolve we rejoice together,
and by the merit of this rejoicing, may all defilements and impurities be extinguished.
Karmic obstacles will be utterly extinguished without remainder, And one will swiftly attain unsurpassed enlightenment.
If you delight in approaching Bodhi, Subduing Māra and adorning your marks, Diligently cultivate this dhāraṇī;
Then that which you desire shall not be difficult to obtain.
If one were to fill as many buddha-fields as there are grains of sand in the Ganges with precious jewels and offer them to a bodhisattva who upholds this sutra,
their merit would exceed that [of the former offering].
Thus spoke the Buddha to Śāriputra.
If a bodhisattva focuses their mind on reciting this dhāraṇī,
eight yakṣas shall constantly provide protection. What are these eight?
The first is named Śuṇṭha;
the second is named Cchada;
the third is named Bāhudanti.
The fourth is named Nārāyaṇabha;
the fifth is named Cchridata;
the sixth is named Tudatsan.
The seventh is named Kumuda;
the eighth is named Subhūṣaṇa.
These eight yakṣas dwell on the Snowy Mountains.
I shall protect and mind these people, supporting their work on the Path;
I shall eliminate their misfortunes and ailments, and increase their vital energy.
Those who uphold this sutra should bathe and put on clean clothing.
One should practice walking meditation, recite, and study this dhāraṇī;
maintain a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings,
contemplate the meaning of the sutras, and make offerings in accordance with the Dharma.
Furthermore, there are eight bodhisattvas dwelling in the heavens of the desire realm who also constantly protect those who uphold this sutra.
What are these eight?
The first is named Rucaka;
the second is named Vairācana;
the third is named Pañcapaṭṭika.
The fourth is named Suyāga-vī;
the fifth is named Satī;
the sixth is named Avibhaya-pa-bon.
The seventh is named Nakṣatrarāja;
the eighth is named Cāritramati.
These eight bodhisattvas shall also serve as his protectors.
To support their progress on the path and enable them to attain this Dharma,
those who uphold this dhāraṇī should honor it,
believe in it, accept it, and practice it accordingly.
Out of compassion for sentient beings, they abandon their faults and evils;
though they receive even slight kindness, they always keep in mind the desire to repay it;
and regarding the profound Dharma, they single-mindedly seek understanding and liberation.
By means of skillful expedients, he constantly benefits sentient beings;
toward those who come to beg, he bestows gifts without parsimony.
When the Tathāgata spoke this Dharma,
There were bodhisattvas, equal in number to the sands of thirty-two Ganges Rivers,
who attained this dhāraṇī and became non-retrogressive from unsurpassed bodhi.
Furthermore, there were sixty Vinbara bodhisattvas who attained the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
Furthermore, thirty-two thousand devas and humans all resolved their minds toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, in this trichiliocosm...
The earth shook in six ways, the devas rained down flowers,
and hundreds of thousands of musical instruments resounded spontaneously without being struck.
At that time, the Elder Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Blessed One, what is the name of this sutra, and how should it be upheld?
The Buddha told Śāriputra,
"This sutra is named the 'Dhāraṇī of the Emergence of Boundless Gates.'"
It is also called the "Dhāraṇī for Attaining Bodhi," and it is also called the "Dhāraṇī for Attaining All-Knowledge and Subduing All Māras.
One should receive and uphold it in this manner.
At that time, when the World-Honored One had finished preaching this sutra,
the Elder Śāriputra, the bodhisattvas who had come from other lands,
and the eight classes of beings— gods, nāgas, and others, both human and non-human— [all rejoiced].
Having heard what the Buddha had spoken, they rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
*The Sūtra of the Dhāraṇī of the Emergence of Boundless Gateways*.
